articles.title: A Seattle shipbuilder sold his company for a reported $3.5 million in 1906 and built an Orcas Island estate; 15 years later he donated more than 2,700 acres to Washington to create Moran State Park
articles.summary: When former Seattle mayor and shipbuilding businessman Robert Moran was told by doctors in 1905 that he had only a few months to live because of a failing
articles.body: When former Seattle mayor and shipbuilding businessman Robert Moran was told by doctors in 1905 that he had only a few months to live because of a failing heart, he decided to spend his remaining time building a peaceful home on Orcas Island in the Pacific Northwest. That diagnosis turned out to be wrong. Moran lived for another 38 years and left behind one of the largest gifts of private land in Washington State.Rise of a Seattle titanMoran arrived in Seattle in 1875 at age 18, with almost nothing. He worked his way up from ship engineer to master mechanic. He later joined his brothers to create Moran Brothers Company, a marine repair business that grew quickly as shipping expanded across the region. His role in Seattle's public life also grew. Moran was elected mayor in 1888 and served two terms, helping lead the city as it rebuilt after the Great Seattle Fire of 1889. The high point of his business career came in 1904, when his shipyard launched the USS Nebraska, the only battleship built in Washington state. According to historical records published by HistoryLink, the ship helped establish Moran as one of the leading shipbuilders in the Pacific Northwest. In 1906, after years of intense work and serious exhaustion, Moran sold the shipbuilding company to a New York group for a reported $3.5 million and retired.Retreat to Orcas IslandLooking for a quieter life, Moran bought thousands of acres on Orcas Island, the largest island in the San Juan Archipelago. Between 1906 and 1909, he oversaw the building of Rosario, a 54-room Arts and Crafts style mansion overlooking East Sound. The family moved into the house on June 21, 1909. The estate had advanced features for its time. Moran built a hydroelectric system to provide electricity, along with workshops where skilled craftsmen made many of the home's features. Shipbuilders and machinists who had worked for Moran Brothers Company helped build the mansion. Its materials included teak, mahogany, and large Belgian glass windows. The island climate appeared to agree with Moran. His health improved, and his attention gradually turned to protecting the forests, lakes, and mountains around his home. He did not allow logging or hunting on his property and began thinking about how the land could one day be preserved for public use.Creating a public parkBy the early 1910s, Moran was concerned about protecting the forests around Mount Constitution, the highest point in the San Juan Islands. He first considered giving the state a small piece of land near the summit. In 1911, he offered about 3,000 acres, including most of the mountain, if the state would also buy some nearby land. The state did not accept the offer at first. Washington had no properly funded agency able to take on and manage such a large park. Moran later reduced the proposed gift to 2,731 acres and removed his conditions. In 1921, the state finally accepted his offer. On April 21, 1921, the State Parks Committee formally accepted nearly 2,700 acres from Moran to create Moran State Park. Washington State Parks records confirm that Moran's gift created one of the state's first major state parks and gave the new state park system a large public land base. Moran wanted the land to be available for public enjoyment. He continued supporting the park after the donation, spending his own money on roads, trails, bridges, and other improvements. Moran also pushed for better access to Mount Constitution. He supported replacing the rough road to the summit with a road suitable for automobiles, helping make it easier for visitors to reach the mountain and its views.Legacy during the Great DepressionDuring the 1930s, Moran State Park became an important work site for the Civilian Conservation Corps, part of President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal. A CCC camp opened at the park in June 1933. Crews built roads, trails, bridges, picnic shelters, and other structures using local materials. The CCC also built the stone observation tower at the top of Mount Constitution. Designed by Seattle architect Ellsworth Storey, the tower was completed in 1936 and stands 53 feet high. From the summit, visitors can see wide views across the San Juan Islands, Puget Sound, Mount Baker, and surrounding mountains. Moran died in 1943 at age 86, nearly four decades after doctors had warned him that he had only months to live. Today, Moran State Park covers more than 5,000 acres and includes five freshwater lakes and more than 30 miles of hiking trails. It is the fourth-largest state park in Washington and remains one of the major public recreation areas in the San Juan Islands. The park protects the forests, lakes, and mountain landscape that Moran began working to preserve more than a century ago.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: U2 celebrate 50th anniversary at the school where they formed
articles.summary: The rock band go back to their roots, playing a gig in the Dublin playground where they first met.
articles.body:
Exactly 50 years after they formed, U2 returned to Dublin to play a gig at the school where they met.

”We‘ve escaped from the lab,” declared Bono, as they quartet took to a stage in the playground. “How’s the experiment working for you?”

The pupils of Mount Temple Comprehensive may not have been born when U2 were the world’s biggest band, but they gave them a hero's welcome, waving signs that said, “I love U2“, “It’s a beautiful day - no school”, and, “Bono, my mum says hi!”

The group treated them to a career-spanning set that included hits like I Will Follow, Vertigo and With Or Without You, as well as their latest single, Silencio.

As they played, teachers pulled down pupils who’d climbed on their classmates' shoulders, before getting swept up in the moment and dancing along themselves.

As he looked out from the same stage where U2 made their debut in 1976, Bono became emotional.

“Thanks for, er… Yeah... I didn’t… Wow,” said the frontman, temporarily lost for words.

The U2 story began in those same halls and corridors five decades ago, when 14-year-old Larry Mullen Jr pinned a handwritten note to the school noticeboard.

Auditions were held a couple of days later, on 25 September, 1976, in Larry's parents' kitchen.

Among the hopeful "misfits", as their school-friend Frank Kearns called them, were Bono, The Edge and Adam Clayton – who arrived wearing a full-length Afghan coat.

Initially called Feedback, and then The Hype, they conquered the world as U2, transforming themselves from a scrappy punk outfit into stadium-conquering rock titans, whose big ideas and big anthems attracted millions of admirers, and almost as many detractors.

Speaking to BBC News, Mullen confessed the infamous wanted advert had been his father's idea all along.

"I'd been playing on my own, in my house, and my dad was pretty frustrated," he says.

"I wasn't very good at many things, and playing the drums was included in that. So I think he, out of frustration, said I should try and play with other people."

"And unfortunately," adds Bono, "he got the three of us."

Bono, then known as Paul Hewson, had actually been tempted to skip the audition. He was two years older, and concerned about looking out of place.

"I wouldn't be hanging out with second years, and particularly really good-looking ones," he says.

Eventually, his friend Reggie Manuel persuaded him to attend, even giving him a lift on his rickety old motorbike.

"I can tell myself it was a Harley Davidson," the singer jokes, "but really it was a Yamaha DX100."

The first band practice didn't exactly show promise.

There was more talking than playing. Clayton, a bassist who couldn't play bass, was selected on account of having "the best hair". And Bono, who wanted to be the guitarist, didn't bring a guitar.

"I was never any good with gear," he reflects. "Carrying it, unpacking it, that kind of thing."

Even so, there were signs the band would attract an adoring legion of fans. Half-way through the rehearsal, a group of screaming girls tried to climb the garden wall.

For Clayton, that was the moment that sealed the deal.

"Larry already had a fan club, and we thought, 'Well, if he's got a fan club, that looks pretty good to us. Maybe if we hang out with this guy, it might stretch a little further'."

Mullen, forever the band's stoic moral compass, was not impressed by the invasion.

"As I recall, Larry Mullen took a hose to the fans," laughs Bono.

"I don't know what possessed me," the drummer grimaces, while trying to insist the hosing "was an act of kindness and love because it was a hot day".

"They enjoyed it," he protests. "It was playful."

Bono jumps in to save his friend's embarrassment…. Well, kind of.

"It's been the story of our lives ever since. He doesn't even want to have fans, but we quite like them."

From that kitchen in Rosemount Avenue, U2 became the world's biggest rock band.

Anthems like With Or Without You, One and Beautiful Day have always sounded majestic yet personal; powered by The Edge's cascading guitar tone and Bono's lyrics which, for all their proselytising, remain grounded in a belief in humanity.

They made a stylistic swerve in the 1990s, embracing electronics, dance music and irony on the albums Achtung Baby, Zooropa and Pop.

Along the way, they reinvented stadium concerts with the Zoo TV tour, whose stage was crammed full of multimedia screens and satellite feeds, while Bono made nightly prank calls to the White House.

The Edge, real name Dave Evans, puts their longevity down to a lack of formal training.

"It's been a guiding light, in some ways, the limitations of the band," he explains.

"We're in this place where, musically, we never know what's about to happen. It can fall apart or it can become something extraordinary.

Back on stage at Mount Temple, Bono paid tribute to his alma matter for allowing the band to flourish.

The support of teachers allowed them to realise that “maybe all we needed was around us, just under our feet,” he said.

And he dedicated the performance to school councillor Jack Heaslip, who later became a “travelling pastor” on the band’s tours, before his death from motor neurone disease in 2015.

U2 then closed their set with an orchestral arrangement of One, assisted by students from Ireland's Music Generation education programme, which they helped fund and establish 15 years ago.

A few hours earlier, the band announced their 16th studio album, Carnaval de Luz, which will be released in November.

It's a companion piece to February's angry, impassioned EP, Days of Ash, which tackled headlines about ICE killings in America, the war in Ukraine and the Israel-Palestine conflict.

That was followed by the more sedate Easter Lily EP in April; with Carnaval de Luz rounding off the story.

The Edge described it as "a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs", while Bono promised "loud guitars, deep bass [and] ecstatic rhythms."

Closing out the album's 12 tracks is Torn, a song co-written by Dolly Parton, which was the country icon's final recorded performance before her death last month.

In a press release, the track was described as "a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances".

BBC News will run an interview about that song, and the rest of the album, in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Trump-Xi bonhomie set to continue, leaders announce two more meetings
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet twice more this year, with the two leaders agreeing to hold talks in China in
articles.body: US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet twice more this year, with the two leaders agreeing to hold talks in China in November and again at the G20 summit in Miami in December, after Xi's three-day state visit to Washington ended on Friday.Trump said Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, had left Washington and were heading back to China, describing their talks as a meeting of “Friendship, Strength, and Success” for both countries.“We will be meeting again in November, in China, and then at the G20 in December, in Miami, Florida,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “Much has been, and will be, accomplished. I look forward to our next meeting!”Xi had invited Trump and first lady Melania Trump to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November. He also said the two leaders could meet again in December at the G20 summit at Trump's National Doral golf club in Miami.“We do welcome Mr. President and the first lady to visit China,” Xi said.Trump responded, “We will, and we’ll be speaking a lot.”Summit ends with no major breakthroughThe latest meeting was held as the US and China sought to maintain a stable relationship between the world's two largest economies. However, the summit did not produce major breakthroughs on issues including trade and the safety of artificial intelligence.The two leaders held a 90-minute closed-door meeting on Thursday. According to the Chinese government's readout, they discussed the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula. The White House did not release details of those talks.Xi's final day in WashingtonBefore leaving the US, Trump took Xi to the National Archives, where the Declaration of Independence, the US Constitution and the Bill of Rights are held.Trump said he wanted to show Xi “some of the greatest treasures of that proud history” as the US marks its 250th anniversary.The two leaders also visited exhibits highlighting the history of US-China relations. Trump had earlier shown Xi a copy of the Declaration of Independence displayed in the Oval Office.“Just as our ancestors reached across the ocean centuries ago to trade, to learn, and to build a better world, our two countries do really the same thing, and we’re very proud of it,” Trump said.Xi's visit also included a meeting with Trump and Melania Trump at the White House, as well as a state dinner attended by technology industry leaders. Melania Trump and Peng visited the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art.The visit came during China's Mid-Autumn Festival, when families traditionally gather to mark the end of the harvest.The high-profile welcome for Xi came as Trump campaigns ahead of the November US midterm elections, during which he has sought to portray Democrats as communists. articles.body: Jaipur: Security arrangements in reserved AC coaches have come under scrutiny after four suspected members of an interstate gang were arrested in connection with an alleged robbery involving cash and jewellery worth around Rs 1 crore aboard Madurai-Bikaner Anuvrat Superfast Express.The case has raised questions over passenger verification and security checks inside reserved coaches, particularly on long-distance trains where passengers frequently board and alight at intermediate stations.Investigators said the accused allegedly remained inside the AC coach for more than an hour without being checked. During this period, they allegedly observed passengers and targeted those carrying valuables.Circle inspector, GRP Bikaner, Neha Rajpurohit, while talking to TOI Friday, said the investigation so far indicated that the suspects had specifically targeted passengers carrying jewellery and cash. “They remained inside the AC coach, observed passengers and allegedly stole valuables from their luggage,” she said.During interrogation, the accused allegedly told investigators that they had remained inside the train for more than an hour and were not checked during that period. Police said the arrested suspects have also confessed to involvement in baggage thefts on trains.Danish Ali, who was travelling from Jaipur Junction to Abu Road on Ashram Express, said stronger verification could improve passenger safety. “Ticket checking primarily establishes the validity of the journey. articles.summary: CU and JU urge West Bengal govt to scrap WBJEE online decentralised counselling and allow offline spot counselling as 370+ BTech seats remain vacant.
articles.body: Kolkata: Vice-chancellors of two state-run universities — Jadavpur University (JU) and Calcutta University (CU) — have urged the state govt to scrap the WBJEE online decentralised counselling and allow the universities to conduct the traditional offline decentralised counselling to fill up the large number of vacant seats.CU has over 140 seats vacant after two phases of online decentralised counselling, nearly 30% of its total BTech seats. JU has over 230 BTech seats vacant, which is around 19% of the total number. There are 478 engineering seats at CU and 1,190 BTech seats at JU. Additionally, there are hundreds of seats vacant in govt engineering colleges across the state.This is the first time that West Bengal Joint Entrance Examination Board is conducting online decentralised counselling in a centralised way. Earlier, decentralised counselling for BTech courses against vacancies used to be conducted by the respective institutions based on WBJEE ranks.JU VC Chiranjib Bhattacharjee said, “I have written to the higher education department to allow us to conduct offline decentralised counselling immediately to fill the vacant seats based on ranks. It is causing a loss for the state and affecting the reputation of the university. We have over 230 vacancies, but we have decided to start our first-year engineering classes from Sept 28.”CU VC Asutosh Ghosh said, “We are concerned about the vacant seats across engineering courses as classes have started. We have asked the state govt whether decentralised counseling could be conducted offline, as in previous years, to fill these seats. We will write to the state govt soon.”In the last few years, 150-180 seats remained vacant at JU after the centralised counselling, which the university filled during decentralised counselling. The situation was similar for CU, where 20-30 seats remained vacant after centralised counselling and was filled up during decentralised counselling by the university.A higher education department official said, “No decision has been made yet on subsequent phases of decentralised counselling. The phase 2 online decentralised counselling ends on Friday. Once we get the seat matrix of vacant seats, we will decide on the next course of action. The whole process is being conducted in a fair and transparent way to ensure there is no merit violation.”VC of Maulana Abul Kalam Azad University of Technology (MAKAUT) Tapas Chakraborty said, “First-year classes should start early so that the teaching-learning process is not hampered.”Engineering professors at both JU and CU feel that without offline decentralised counselling, the vacant seats will not be completely filled.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.title: A Minnesota family farm has been sold to a homebuilder and grading has already begun; the city has now given final approval to turn the 88-acre property into a 262-home community by 2032
articles.summary: Heavy machinery has already started moving soil across a historic family farm in Minnesota.
articles.body: Heavy machinery has already started moving soil across a historic family farm in Minnesota. The work is preparing the property for a large new housing development after city officials gave final approval to the plans. The Prior Lake City Council unanimously approved the final plat, planned unit development, and development agreement for the former Vierling family farmstead. Pulte Homes of Minnesota recently bought the 88-acre property. It will become a 262-home neighborhood called Vierling Ridge, with the full development expected to be finished by 2032.Breaking ground on the former farmsteadPeople travelling near County Road 42 and Eagle Creek Avenue in Prior Lake have seen heavy equipment grading the property during the past month. According to documents presented to the council by Casey McCabe, Prior Lake's community development director, general grading work started before final plat approval. The early work was needed to prepare the land for utility installation. Pulte Homes told city officials that it plans to finish the main infrastructure during the autumn. That schedule will allow builders to begin work on model homes and townhouses during the winter. The company hopes to have the first homes ready for the spring housing market. The project was first presented to city planners as Marlow Ridge. It was later renamed Vierling Ridge at Scott County's request. The county wanted the public records to clearly show the property's historical ownership.Phased layout and housing optionsThe development is planned to offer different types of homes for people at different stages of life. It will include several housing styles and price ranges. Planners estimate that the project will have an overall density of 3.75 homes per acre. The options will include single-level twin homes for couples and buyers aged 55 and older, traditional townhouses for first-time buyers, and detached single-family homes in different sizes. The first construction phase will cover 18 acres of the property. About 12 acres will be used for homes and local roads. Nearly six acres will be used for public rights-of-way. The first phase calls for 12 twin homes, 12 townhomes, and 22 detached single-family homes. It will also include completing Fountain Hills Drive to Eagle Creek Avenue and building Surrey Lane. The new lane will connect Carriage Hills Parkway with Fountain Hills Drive. The second phase is planned to take two years and continue through 2028. The remaining homes will then be built in stages, with the entire project expected to be completed by 2032.Financial and infrastructure detailsIn documents prepared for the council meeting, McCabe said the mix of housing types across the 88-acre property would help expand and diversify the city's property tax base. Vierling Ridge will not have its own dedicated parkland. However, two existing community parks are located within a half-mile of the development. Pulte Homes also signed a detailed development agreement with the city. The agreement includes major financial deposits and guarantees for infrastructure work:Public Escrow: More than $873,000 has been placed in a special escrow account. The money will cover public improvements and planned work at the intersection of Eagle Creek Avenue and Fountain Hills Drive.Municipal Fees: About $843,000 in city fees will cover administrative costs, park dedication, street seal coating, trunk sewer work, and water systems.Security Bonds: Pulte has provided nearly $6 million in security guarantees. The guarantees cover sanitary sewer work, storm water systems, water mains, local streets, sidewalks, and pedestrian trails.Council approval and next stepsThe council gave preliminary and final approval for the development plan in June. It then took its final vote on the development agreement and plat details this week. McCabe asked the council to move the item from the consent agenda to the main discussion session. This allowed the council to formally confirm the change to the name Vierling Ridge, as required by Scott County for its administrative records. The council's unanimous vote clears the way for site work and utility installation to continue in the coming months. articles.title: Trump's plans for massive arch move ahead
articles.summary: Opposition to building the 250-foot arch, and using it for military purposes, is growing with one Democrat blasting Trump's plans as "foolhardy".
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump's plans for building a massive arch appear to be moving ahead, after a federal advisory council terminated talks on how to handle the 250-foot structure's possible effects on nearby historic sites.

The council, led by Trump appointees, announced on Thursday it was ending required consultations on the project, saying historic preservation officers from Washington and Virginia had refused to sign off on harm-mitigation plans.

Construction was already expected to begin this month, but opposition has been growing.

On Friday, Democratic Senator Tammy Duckworth blasted plans to use the arch for defence as "foolhardy" and called it "yet another Trump vanity project".

Earlier this week Trump announced that the proposed "Triumphal Arch" would double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones from the roof and plaza.

In a letter to the Pentagon and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Duckworth said they "must reject this foolhardy plan and instead focus on increasing the safety of the airspace".

The arch is to be built just outside Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, and about 4mi (6km) from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, the site of the deadly 2025 midair crash between a military helicopter and commercial plane.

"The American people cannot afford to stand witness to Trump's risky plan to place a 250-foot (72m) structure along a busy approach path, especially if he follows through on plans to station snipers on the arch and fly drones," Duckworth wrote in the letter, which was obtained by the BBC's US partner, CBS News.

The FAA, however, ruled last week that the massive structure would not pose a risk to flights coming into and out of the airport.

On Thursday, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, led by Trump appointees, announced it was ending required consultations with local officials about how the structure might affect 42 historic properties in the area.

The council said in the announcement that the National Park Service, which oversees federal landmarks, had proposed a plan for mitigating potential harms to those properties, but local historic preservation officers "raised concerns with the purpose and need of the Triumphal Arch". They also questioned whether the service had adequately identified possible harms and planned sufficient actions to address them.

Federal and state officials are not required to reach an agreement on a project's harm-mitigation plans, and those consultations are allowed to be terminated if both sides can't agree. The council expects to submit a final report on the process early next month.

Meanwhile, Democratic Virginia Congressman Don Beyer says excavation work on the site where the arch will stand has already begun.

Beyer, who is leading congressional opposition to the arch, said he found workers operating heavy equipment when he visited the site on Thursday who told him they were "conducting archaeological work to evaluate the composition of the soil".

That is "deeply troubling", Beyer said, particularly because the administration is required to give 48 hours notice before work can begin.

"The Administration appears to be pushing ahead with activity at the site even while it still has not done the basic work necessary to understand the consequences of this project," Beyer wrote.

A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.

articles.title: Penn’s Cave and Wildlife Park seeks new owner for first time since 1908, with historic 1,400-acre Pennsylvania property listed at an asking price of $34 million
articles.summary: Penn’s Cave and Wildlife Park in Pennsylvania is seeking a new owner for the first time in 118 years, with the 1,400-acre property listed at an asking
articles.body: Penn’s Cave and Wildlife Park in Pennsylvania is seeking a new owner for the first time in 118 years, with the 1,400-acre property listed at an asking price of $34 million. The Campbell family, which has owned and operated the Centre County attraction since 1908, announced Wednesday that it will begin accepting proposals from potential buyers on October 1.The property includes Penn’s Cave, described as the only all-water cavern and wildlife park in the United States. Owners Russ and Jeanne Schleiden said the decision to seek a buyer was not taken lightly, stressing that maintaining the attraction and its natural resources remains a priority during the transition.“Penn’s Cave has been our family’s legacy. We have a lot of pride in this property and the business,” the owners said in a written statement quoted by the Centre Daily Times. They added that the family would continue maintaining the property with the same level of commitment while searching for its next owner.“Continuing the experience we’re known for is our greatest priority throughout this transition,” they said.Historic cave draws visitors from around the worldEstimated to be about 30 million years old, Penn’s Cave is a roughly quarter-mile-long natural limestone cave featuring guided boat tours. It is the only cave in Pennsylvania listed on the National Register of Historic Places.A nomination form dating to 1883 described the cave’s formations as “varied and fantastic to an extraordinary degree” and called it a “picturesquely beautiful spectacle.” The document also described Penn’s Cave and its boat tours as the most widely known tourist attraction in Centre County and among the most popular attractions in Pennsylvania.The business says millions of people from around the world have visited Penn’s Cave during its nearly 150-year history.According to a company press release, four generations of the Campbell family have worked to preserve the property, establish water rights and acquire surrounding land to support the continued stewardship of its natural resources. The property generates as much as 11 million gallons of water each day.Wildlife park features native and exotic speciesBeyond the cave, the property includes a wildlife park that is home to a range of animals, including bison, Texas longhorns, elk, white-tailed deer, wild horses, donkeys, mountain lions and wolves.Other attractions include a maze, gemstone panning, picnic grounds and off-road mountain tours. The property also has a private airport that allows pilots and their passengers to arrive directly at the attraction.The family said finding a new owner who understands the property’s potential and is committed to its long-term stewardship will be central to the sale process.“Preserving the business and finding the next steward of the land who can see the immense potential of the property and continue the legacy” are among the family’s priorities.Potential state park deal had been consideredThe sale announcement comes roughly two months after the family revealed that it was considering selling the property to Pennsylvania’s Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.The proposal would have turned Penn’s Cave into Pennsylvania’s 126th state park and received support from Centre County commissioners and state Rep. Kerry Benninghoff. However, the state budget was passed without legislation that would have facilitated the transfer.During a July commissioners meeting, Benninghoff said several investors had expressed interest in purchasing the property and dividing it into multiple parcels for development. He described that possibility as “a real shame.”It remains unclear whether Gov. Josh Shapiro’s administration continues to have an interest in acquiring the property. Benninghoff has said he would introduce legislation for the transfer again if he is reelected.Antique machinery show’s future also uncertainThe possible sale has also raised questions about the future of the Nittany Antique Machinery Association’s events at Penn’s Cave. The organization’s shows are billed as the largest antique machinery shows on the East Coast, with the annual event dating back to 1975.The association has been seeking a five-year lease renewal. Penn’s Cave, however, sought a one-year lease with new conditions, according to court documents.In a letter included in a court filing, Penn’s Cave said its plans for the property were a “strong consideration” in its lease negotiations. The existing lease expires on December 31.The association withdrew its request for judicial intervention on Monday, saying it hopes the move will create an opportunity for constructive negotiations between the two organizations.“We respect Penn’s Cave and understand that it has interests and decisions to make regarding its property,” association President Doug Leitch said in a written statement. “Our hope is that both sides can put those interests on the table, listen to one another and find common ground.”Proposals for the 1,400-acre Penn’s Cave and Wildlife Park will be accepted beginning October 1, as the Campbell family begins the process of determining who will take over the historic Pennsylvania attraction.You use AI every day.
